hook: A bakery buys eggs by the dozen because counting them one at a time is slow. Atoms are far too small to count at all: a single drop of water holds more molecules than there are stars in the visible universe. Chemists count them by weighing, using a counting unit called the mole.

prereq.q: Which conversion factor turns grams into kilograms?
prereq.why: The unit you want goes on top, so grams cancel: 1 kg / 1000 g.

prereq.q: How many significant figures does 0.0450 have?
prereq.why: Leading zeros never count; the trailing zero after a decimal point does: 4, 5, 0.

chain.cause: Atoms are too small to count one by one
chain.effect: chemists count them in groups of 6.022 × 10²³, called a mole

chain.cause: The mole is defined so that 12 amu per atom matches 12 g per mole
chain.effect: the atomic mass in amu equals the molar mass in g/mol

chain.cause: A balance measures grams, and molar mass is grams per mole
chain.effect: dividing a mass by the molar mass gives moles

chain.cause: Each mole holds Avogadro's number of particles
chain.effect: multiplying moles by 6.022 × 10²³ gives the number of particles

ideas: One mole is 6.022 × 10²³ particles; say which particles you mean.
Molar mass (g/mol) is the sum of the atomic masses in one particle.
Mass ↔ moles uses molar mass; moles ↔ particles uses Avogadro's number.
Report the answer with the significant figures of the least precise measurement.

misconception.wrong: Equal masses of two substances hold equal numbers of molecules.
misconception.right: Molecules of different substances have different masses, so equal masses usually hold different numbers of molecules. Compare amounts in moles.

summary: Chemists count atoms and molecules in moles of 6.022 × 10²³ particles. The molar mass, in grams per mole, links a measured mass to an amount in moles, and Avogadro's number links moles to particles.
